newsitem.title: USA: Public hearing into TWA 800 crash planned for December.
newsitem.headline: Public hearing into TWA 800 crash planned for December.

text.p: A public hearing into the 1996 crash of TWA Flight 800 is planned for December in Baltimore, the nation's top safety investigator said on Thursday.

In prepared testimony to a House Transportation subcommittee, National Transportation Safety Board Chairman Jim Hall said the board still had months of tests and research into the accident ahead of it.
On the evening of July 17, 1996, the TWA Boeing 747 exploded over the Atlantic Ocean near Long Island on its way from New York to Paris. All 230 people on board were killed.
Early suspicions of a bomb or missile touching off the blast faded as the investigation ground on.

"All of our efforts to date have failed to uncover any credible evidence that the loss of Flight 800 was the result of a criminal act," Federal Bureau of Investigation official James Kallstrom said in prepared remarks to the same panel.
Kallstrom said the FBI had not reached the end of its investigation but said his organisation was close to conclusion.
"Barring some new disclosure or information, we are now in the final phase of our investigation," he said.
NTSB's Hall reiterated that the board was focusing on the explosion of the fuel and air vapours in the TWA 800's centre fuel tank.
"We have not yet determined what ignited the fuel vapour in the centre tank," Hall said. But he said there was no evidence of a bomb or missile impact in the wreckage.

Hall said the hearings in Baltimore would take sworn testimony on the accident but the NTSB could not conduct a hearing until the FBI declared it was no longer conducting a criminal investigation. "We anticipate that they may do so in the near future," he said.

Hall said safety officials were pursuing a number of theories on how the centre fuel tank ignited, including overheating of the tank's scavenge pump, static electricity, a short circuit in a fuel probe and degrading of wires.

Also being pursued, Hall said, was the possibility of a small explosive charge near the centre tank and the possibility of a high speed particle such as a fragment from a meteorite, space debris or a missile warhead.
In late July and early August the NTSB will set off small explosive charges around a centre wing tank of a retired Boeing 747 in England as part of its continuing tests.

The board leased a Boeing 747 for flight tests to examine various temperature and vapour concentrations under conditions similar to those of TWA 800. The board may blow up one or more centre tanks salvaged from retired Boeing 747s.
Hall repeated his disappointment with the Federal Aviation Administration for failing to adopt interim measures to prevent similar explosions.
